case.label: B
case.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration also speeds up downloads from a bucket over the AWS edge network, so a candidate could argue it reduces wait time with only a bucket setting. It fails because it does not cache: every download still reaches us-east-1, and the stem stresses images that rarely change, which is the signal for caching.

case.label: B
case.text: A CloudWatch alarm plus a script that swaps the origin also fails over to the replica bucket and works for a read-only site. It needs custom code, a slow origin update and an alarm delay, so it loses on the least-overhead constraint and on speed; the other options fail on feasibility (Global Accelerator has no S3 endpoints).

case.label: D
case.text: Copying the assets to the EC2 instances and using one distribution with the load balancer origin gives one domain, edge caching of assets and uncached /api/*. It works technically but adds a copy and sync job and moves static hosting onto instances, so it has more overhead than using the existing bucket as a second origin.

case.label: D
case.text: Signed URLs are the classic way to give temporary access, and a website could generate one per segment. It fails the stated constraint that the player URLs must not change (and hundreds of segments per video), which is exactly what signed cookies solve.

answers.flag: Option E (a viewer-request CloudFront function that strips cookies, User-Agent and other query strings) would also normalize the cache key before lookup and could replace B in a valid pair (D plus E), though with more overhead than a cache policy; the stem does not say that cache-policy editing is the only way, so the key rests on the overhead wording.

case.label: E
case.text: A CloudFront function on the viewer request event runs before the cache lookup, so removing cookies, User-Agent and extra query strings makes requests identical and raises the hit ratio at very low cost. It is defensible as an alternative to B, but it is custom code to maintain, whereas a cache policy does the same by configuration.

case.label: D
case.text: NLBs with Elastic IP addresses give static IPs, and Route 53 failover records with health checks move traffic between Regions, so the partners could allow-list the NLB addresses of both Regions. It is slower because failover depends on DNS caching and TTLs, and the partners would need both Regions' address sets; Global Accelerator moves traffic without DNS.

case.label: C
case.text: Lambda@Edge on the viewer request event can read Accept-Language and rewrite the URI, so it is functionally correct. It costs more per request than a CloudFront function for a tiny header-based rewrite on every request, so it loses on the most-cost-effective wording.

case.label: B
case.text: One invalidation for /* counts as one path and is cheap, so the charges could stop growing. It does not fix copies held by browsers and corporate proxies, which the stem names, and it still needs a step on every deployment, so it does not give users the new files right after each deployment.

case.label: A
case.text: Restricting the security group to the CloudFront managed prefix list is the common low-effort protection and limits who can connect. The load balancer stays internet-facing in public subnets, which the stem says must end.

case.label: D
case.text: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers with one setting and one URL change. It adds a per-GB acceleration charge and caches nothing, so millions of downloads of the same files do not get cheaper, while CloudFront serves them from cache.

case.label: D
case.text: A CloudFront function on viewer request is the cheapest compute at the edge and runs for every request. It cannot call DynamoDB over the network, and the stem fixes the blocklist in a DynamoDB table; a key-value store option would change the data location, which the stem does not allow.

case.label: C
case.text: Route 53 latency-based records send each player to the closest Region by DNS and are cheap. They do not give fixed IP addresses, do not use the AWS network between edge and Region, and DNS caching limits failover, so they do not give the lowest latency for UDP traffic.

case.label: C
case.text: HTTPS Only in the viewer protocol policy sounds like it secures the whole path and is a one-click change. It affects only the viewer-to-CloudFront connection; the origin protocol policy controls the second connection, and the load balancer has no HTTPS listener.

case.label: B
case.text: Adding no-store and private on the origin response looks like the direct way to stop caching. The minimum TTL of the custom policy overrides origin no-cache style directives, so it would not help while the policy keeps the 3600 seconds.

case.label: C
case.text: A daily Lambda function that rewrites security group rules from the published IP ranges also limits access to CloudFront addresses. It duplicates what the managed prefix list does automatically, so it has more overhead; it also would not prove the request came from this distribution, which the secret header does.

answers.flag: A and C are parallel (dial 0 on the standby endpoint group versus weight 0 on its endpoint), and the key depends on the documented behavior of a traffic dial or weight of zero during failover, which the stem does not state; a candidate who believes weight 0 also keeps a standby could defend C in place of A.

case.label: C
case.text: Setting the us-west-2 endpoint weight to 0 also keeps normal traffic in us-east-1 and is a per-endpoint setting. Weights only split traffic between endpoints inside one endpoint group, so they do not choose between Regions; the traffic dial is the control that does.

answers.flag: The stem names no constraint that excludes an origin access identity (such as SSE-KMS or a newer Region), so a candidate who knows an OAI can pass PUT requests in many Regions could defend D; the key rests on OAC being the current method.

case.label: D
case.text: An origin access identity with a bucket policy also restricts the bucket to the distribution and can allow PUT, so the stem could be met with it. It is the legacy method with limits, and OAC is the recommended and complete one.

case.label: B
case.text: Signed URLs with a trusted key group would stop direct S3 access if the bucket is also private. The stem says every visitor can download, so per-user signing adds code for no requirement, and the bucket lock itself is done by origin access control.

case.label: B
case.text: Requesting both certificates in the Region where the application runs is a natural guess and is right for the load balancer. A certificate for the distribution must be in US East (N. Virginia), so the distribution part fails.

case.label: C
case.text: Launching a patched fleet and swapping it into the endpoint group also gives near-zero downtime without touching traffic dials. It builds a whole new fleet and load balancer for a restart-only patch, so it has more overhead than turning the dial down.

answers.flag: The stem does not say the patch files are served by the game-server NLBs or that HTTPS is terminated there, and Global Accelerator also speeds up HTTPS, so a candidate could defend A; the key rests on the signal that weekly-changing large files are cacheable.

case.label: A
case.text: Global Accelerator lowers latency for any TCP traffic, including HTTPS, to the nearest healthy Region and the question asks about response times for players far from both Regions in general. It does not cache, so repeated downloads of the same weekly patch still cross to the origin Region.

case.label: D
case.text: Origin access control with a bucket policy for the service principal restricts reads to the distribution. The stem says this is already in place, and it gives no paid-customer or time-limited control, so it does not add the missing requirement.
